## III

There was music from my neighbour's house through the summer nights. In his blue gardens men and girls came and went like moths among the whisperings and the champagne and the stars. At high tide I watched his guests diving from the tower of his raft or taking the sun on the hot sand of his beach, while his two motorboats slit the waters of the Sound. On weekends his Rolls-Royce became an omnibus, bearing parties to and from the city, while his station wagon scampered like a brisk yellow bug to meet all trains. On Mondays eight servants toiled all day repairing the ravages of the night before.

Every Friday five crates of oranges and lemons arrived from a fruiterer in New York—every Monday these same oranges and lemons left his back door in a pyramid of pulpless halves. There was a machine in the kitchen that could extract the juice of two hundred oranges in half an hour if a butler's thumb pressed a little button two hundred times.

At least once a fortnight a corps of caterers came down with several hundred feet of canvas and enough coloured lights to make a Christmas tree of Gatsby's garden. On buffet tables spiced baked hams crowded against pastry pigs and turkeys bewitched to a dark gold, and a bar with a real brass rail was stocked with gins and cordials so long forgotten that most of his female guests were too young to know one from another.

By seven the orchestra had arrived—no thin five-piece affair, but oboes and trombones and saxophones and viols and cornets and piccolos, low and high drums. The cars from New York were parked five deep in the drive; already the halls and verandas were gaudy with primary colours and hair bobbed in strange new ways, and floating rounds of cocktails permeated the garden until the air was alive with chatter and introductions forgotten on the spot.

The lights grow brighter as the earth lurches away from the sun, and now the orchestra is playing yellow cocktail music, and the opera of voices pitches a key higher. Laughter is easier minute by minute, spilled with prodigality, tipped out at a cheerful word. Groups dissolve and form in the same breath; confident girls weave among the stouter and more stable, become for a sharp, joyous moment the centre of a group, and glide on through the sea-change of faces under the constantly changing light.

Suddenly one of these gypsies, in trembling opal, seizes a cocktail out of the air, dumps it down for courage, and dances out alone on the canvas platform. A momentary hush; a burst of chatter as the erroneous news goes around that she is Gilda Gray's understudy from the Follies. The party has begun.

I believe that on the first night I went to Gatsby's house I was one of the few guests who had actually been invited. People were not invited—they went there. A chauffeur in a uniform of robin's-egg blue had crossed my lawn that Saturday morning with a surprisingly formal note: the honour would be entirely Gatsby's if I would attend his "little party" that night. Signed Jay Gatsby, in a majestic hand.

Dressed in white flannels I went over a little after seven and wandered ill at ease among people I didn't know. I was struck by the number of young Englishmen dotted about—all well dressed, all looking a little hungry, all talking in low earnest voices to solid, prosperous Americans. I was sure they were selling something: bonds or insurance or automobiles. The two or three people of whom I asked my host's whereabouts stared at me in such an amazed way, and denied so vehemently any knowledge of his movements, that I slunk off toward the cocktail table—the only place a single man could linger without looking purposeless and alone.

I was on my way to get roaring drunk from sheer embarrassment when Jordan Baker came out of the house and stood at the head of the marble steps, leaning a little backward and looking with contemptuous interest down into the garden.

"Hello!" I roared, advancing toward her.

"I thought you might be here," she responded absently. Two girls in twin yellow dresses called up from the foot of the steps: "Sorry you didn't win." That was for the golf tournament; she had lost in the finals the week before. With Jordan's slender golden arm resting in mine we descended and sat at a table with the yellow girls and three men, each introduced as Mr. Mumble.

The conversation leaned and whispered. "Somebody told me they thought he killed a man once." A thrill passed over all of us. "I don't think it's so much that," argued Lucille; "it's more that he was a German spy during the war." We all turned and looked around for Gatsby. It was testimony to the romantic speculation he inspired that there were whispers about him from those who had found little that it was necessary to whisper about in this world.

After a wasteful half-hour at a staider East Egg table Jordan whispered, "Let's get out; this is much too polite for me." We tried an important-looking door and walked into a high Gothic library panelled with carved English oak, probably transported complete from some ruin overseas. A stout middle-aged man with enormous owl-eyed spectacles sat somewhat drunk on the edge of a great table, staring at the shelves. As we entered he wheeled excitedly around.

"What do you think?" he demanded, waving at the bookshelves. "I ascertained. They're real."

"The books?"

"Absolutely real—have pages and everything. I thought they'd be a nice durable cardboard. Matter of fact, they're absolutely real." He rushed to the bookcases and returned with Volume One of the Stoddard Lectures. "See! It's a bona-fide piece of printed matter. This fella's a regular Belasco. Knew when to stop, too—didn't cut the pages."

He replaced the book hastily, muttering that if one brick was removed the whole library was liable to collapse, and we shook hands with him gravely and went back outdoors.

There was dancing now on the canvas in the garden: old men pushing young girls backward in eternal graceless circles, superior couples holding each other tortuously, fashionably, in the corners. By midnight the hilarity had increased. A celebrated tenor had sung in Italian, a notorious contralto in jazz, and champagne was served in glasses bigger than finger-bowls. The moon had risen higher, and floating in the Sound was a triangle of silver scales, trembling to the stiff, tinny drip of the banjoes on the lawn.

I was still with Jordan, at a table with a man about my age and a rowdy little girl who gave way upon the slightest provocation to uncontrollable laughter. I had taken two finger-bowls of champagne, and the scene had changed before my eyes into something significant, elemental, and profound.

At a lull the man looked at me and smiled. "Your face is familiar. Weren't you in the First Division during the war?"

"I was in the Twenty-eighth Infantry."

"I was in the Sixteenth until June nineteen-eighteen."

We talked for a moment about wet grey villages in France. He told me he had just bought a hydroplane and was going to try it in the morning. "Want to go with me, old sport?"

It was on the tip of my tongue to ask his name when Jordan turned and smiled. "Having a gay time now?"

"Much better." I turned back. "This is an unusual party for me. I haven't even seen the host. I live over there, and this man Gatsby sent over his chauffeur with an invitation."

For a moment he looked at me as if he failed to understand.

"I'm Gatsby," he said suddenly.

"What! Oh, I beg your pardon."

"I thought you knew, old sport. I'm afraid I'm not a very good host."

He smiled understandingly—much more than understandingly. It was one of those rare smiles with a quality of eternal reassurance in it, that you may come across four or five times in life. It faced—or seemed to face—the whole eternal world for an instant, and then concentrated on you with an irresistible prejudice in your favour. It understood you just so far as you wanted to be understood, believed in you as you would like to believe in yourself, and assured you that it had precisely the impression of you that, at your best, you hoped to convey.
